claim: Superfast muscles (SFMs) are capable of contraction rates up to 250 Hz.
source: Superfast muscles (SFMs) are extremely fast synchronous muscles capable of contraction rates up to 250 Hz, enabling precise motor execution at the millisecond time scale.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a defining characteristic of SFMs.

claim: SFM phenotypes have been discovered in most major vertebrate lineages.
source: SFM phenotypes have been discovered in most major vertebrate lineages, but it remains unknown whether all SFMs share excitation-contraction coupling pathway adaptations for speed, and if SFMs arose once, or from independent evolutionary events.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: Bat and songbird SFM express myosin heavy chain genes that are evolutionarily and ontologically distinct.
source: Here, we demonstrate that to achieve rapid actomyosin crossbridge kinetics bat and songbird SFM express myosin heavy chain genes that are evolutionarily and ontologically distinct.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by phylogenetic analysis and expression data presented in the results.

claim: All known SFMs share multiple functional adaptations that minimize excitation-contraction coupling transduction times.
source: Furthermore, we show that all known SFMs share multiple functional adaptations that minimize excitation-contraction coupling transduction times.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by morphometric and calcium dynamics data in the results.

claim: SFM evolved independently in sound-producing organs in ray-finned fish, birds, and mammals.
source: Our results suggest that SFM evolved independently in sound-producing organs in ray-finned fish, birds, and mammals, and that SFM phenotypes operate at a maximum operational speed set by fundamental constraints in synchronous muscle.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the abstract and supported by the phylogenetic analysis showing non-orthologous MYH genes.

claim: SFM phenotypes operate at a maximum operational speed set by fundamental constraints in synchronous muscle.
source: Our results suggest that SFM evolved independently in sound-producing organs in ray-finned fish, birds, and mammals, and that SFM phenotypes operate at a maximum operational speed set by fundamental constraints in synchronous muscle.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the abstract and supported by the convergence of performance characteristics across independently evolved SFMs.

claim: Fundamental constraints in synchronous muscle set a fundamental limit to the maximum speed of fine motor control.
source: Consequentially, these constraints set a fundamental limit to the maximum speed of fine motor control.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the abstract based on the finding that SFMs operate at maximum speed.

claim: SFMs can produce work at cycling rates over around 90 Hz and up to 250 Hz.
source: Their ability to repetitively contract and relax fast enough to produce work at cycling rates over around 90 Hz and up to 250 Hz sets them apart from other muscles by almost two orders of magnitude and allows the execution of central motor commands with millisecond temporal precision (Rome, 2006; Rome et al., 1988; Elemans et al., 2004, 2008, 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: SFMs have been established in mammals, birds, reptiles, and ray-finned fish.
source: Although once considered an extremely rare muscle phenotype, SFMs have now been established in most major vertebrate lineages (mammals [Elemans et al., 2011], birds [Elemans et al., 2004; Elemans et al., 2008], reptiles [Rome et al., 1996], ray-finned fish [Rome et al., 1996]).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations for each lineage.

claim: SFMs in the bat larynx control the rapid, high frequency calls used by laryngeally echolocating bats.
source: SFMs in the bat larynx control the rapid, high frequency calls used by laryngeally echolocating bats to detect, orient to and track prey (Elemans et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: SFMs in the songbird syrinx control the precisely timed, rapidly produced acoustic elements and frequency sweeps of bird vocalizations.
source: SFMs in the songbird syrinx control the precisely timed, rapidly produced acoustic elements and frequency sweeps of bird vocalizations (Elemans et al., 2004, 2008) used for territorial defense and mate attraction (Collins, 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: SFMs in the Oyster toadfish swimbladder set the fundamental frequency of the produced sound by rhythmically contracting the swimbladder.
source: SFMs in the Oyster toadfish swimbladder and rattlesnake tailshaker both set the fundamental frequency of the produced sound by rhythmically contracting the swimbladder and shaking tail rattles respectively (Rome et al., 1996).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: SFMs in the rattlesnake tailshaker set the fundamental frequency of the produced sound by shaking tail rattles.
source: SFMs in the Oyster toadfish swimbladder and rattlesnake tailshaker both set the fundamental frequency of the produced sound by rhythmically contracting the swimbladder and shaking tail rattles respectively (Rome et al., 1996).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: SFMs have so far been established only in motor systems involving sound production and control.
source: Taken together, SFMs seem a commonly occurring muscle phenotype that interestingly so far has been established only in motor systems involving sound production and control.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction based on the review of known SFM locations.

claim: In swimbladder SFMs, a far greater proportion of cellular volume is dedicated to SR compared to locomotory muscles.
source: In swimbladder SFMs, a far greater proportion of cellular volume is dedicated to SR compared to locomotory muscles, which increases the number and density of SERCA pumps (Rome et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Small, ribbon-like myofibrils in swimbladder SFMs greatly reduce diffusion distances for Ca2+.
source: Furthermore small, ribbon-like myofibrils (Appelt et al., 1991) greatly reduce diffusion distances for Ca2+.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Toadfish swimbladder SFMs have the shortest [Ca2+]i transient times observed in any muscle.
source: Together, these adaptations lead to the shortest [Ca2+]i transient times observed in any muscle (Rome et al., 1996).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: The rate of actomyosin crossbridge detachment in SFM of the toadfish swimbladder is extremely fast.
source: Additionally, the rate of actomyosin crossbridge detachment in SFM of the toadfish swimbladder is extremely fast, which is necessary to ensure a rapid force drop after the return of actin filament inhibition (Rome et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Kinetic tuning of the actomyosin crossbridge cycle is accomplished largely via the differential expression of specific myosin heavy chain (MYH) genes.
source: In vertebrates, kinetic tuning of the actomyosin crossbridge cycle for different energetic and biomechanical requirements is accomplished largely via the differential expression of specific myosin heavy chain (MYH) genes each with unique kinetic properties (Bottinelli et al., 1991).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: The fast actomyosin detachment rate of SFM in the toadfish swimbladder reduces the proportion of myosin motors actively bound to actin at a given time.
source: The fast actomyosin detachment rate of SFM in the toadfish swimbladder, in the absence of a commensurate increase in the rate of crossbridge formation, reduces the proportion of myosin motors actively bound to actin at a given time, and thus force and power production (Rome et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: The increased volumetric allocation for required SR and mitochondria in SFMs leave less space for contractile machinery, reducing volume-specific force and power.
source: Furthermore, the increased volumetric allocation for required SR and mitochondria leave less space for contractile machinery, further reducing volume-specific force and power (Rome and Lindstedt, 1998).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: SFMs in bat, songbird and toadfish develop very similar low force (10–20 kN/m2).
source: SFMs in bat, songbird and toadfish, which produce work up to similar cycling limits (around 200 Hz), develop very similar low force (10–20 kN/m2) (Rome, 2006; Elemans et al., 2004, 2008, 2011; Rome et al., 1996).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Zebra finch syringeal SFM is highly enriched for the MYH13 ortholog transcript.
source: In male zebra finch syrinx SFM, multiple attempts at immunostaining were unsuccessful (see Materials and methods), but sequenced amplicons of qPCR analysis unambiguously showed that it was highly enriched for the MYH13 ortholog transcript (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results and supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: Bat SFM laryngeal muscle is highly enriched for the mammal-lineage-specific MYH4 transcript.
source: In agreement with that, sequenced amplicons of qPCR analysis revealed that bat SFM laryngeal muscle is highly enriched for the mammal-lineage-specific MYH4 transcript, which codes for a locomotory myosin also known as MyHC-2B (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results and supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Bat laryngeal SFM does not express MYH13.
source: Surprisingly, we did not find immunoreactivity against MYH13 in bat laryngeal SFM (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Female zebra finch syringeal SFMs expressed more than five times less MYH13 compared to male syringeal SFMs.
source: Female syringeal SFMs have two-fold slower twitch kinetics than male syringeal SFMs (Elemans et al., 2008), and expressed more than five times less MYH13 compared to male syringeal SFMs (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: MYH13 was significantly upregulated progressively in juvenile male zebra finch syringeal SFM during the sensorimotor phase of vocal learning.
source: Of all MYH genes, only MYH13 changed significantly with age (p=0.02, KW-test) and was significantly upregulated progressively (p<0.05, Tukey-Kramer post hoc) in juvenile male syringeal SFM (Figure 4c).
evidence: This is stated in the results with statistical analysis and supported by data shown in Figure 4c.

claim: Muscle twitch duration significantly decreased progressively during the sensorimotor period of vocal learning in zebra finches.
source: Second, we found that muscle twitch duration significantly decreased progressively (p<0.05, Wilcoxon-signed rank tests) during the sensorimotor period of vocal learning (Figure 4d).
evidence: This is stated in the results with statistical analysis and supported by data shown in Figure 4d.

claim: All SFMs have VPESR ≥15% and SR per myofibril ratio ≥30%.
source: Thus the morphometric cellular adaptation of larger SR volume to increase signal transduction (Rome, 2006; Rome and Lindstedt, 1998) is a hallmark adaptation present in all SFM.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by TEM data shown in Figure 5b.

claim: SR volume was significantly higher in all SFMs compared to intraspecific skeletal muscles in zebra finch, bat and rattlesnake.
source: SR volume was ≥15% and SR per myofibril ratio was ≥30% for all SFMs and significantly higher (p<0.05, KW test) compared to intraspecific skeletal muscles in zebra finch, bat and rattlesnake.
evidence: This is stated in the results with statistical analysis.

claim: At their respective operating temperatures of 39°C and 25°C, the FWHM values of calcium transients for zebra finch syrinx and toadfish swimbladder SFMs did not differ significantly.
source: At their respective operating temperatures of 39°C and 25°C, the full width at half maximum (FWHM) values of calcium transients for zebra finch syrinx and toadfish swimbladder SFMs did not differ significantly (p=0.54, one-tailed paired t-test) and measured 1.98 ± 0.65 ms (N = 4) and 1.91 ± 0.69 ms (N = 2), respectively.
evidence: This is stated in the results with statistical analysis and measurement values.

claim: The FWHM[Ca2+]i in rattle snake tailshaker SFM was 1.5 ms at 35°C.
source: The FWHM[Ca2+]i in rattle snake tailshaker SFM was 1.5 ms at 35°C (Rome et al., 1996).
evidence: This is stated in the results with a citation.

claim: The FWHM[Ca2+]i values for SFMs in zebra finch, toadfish, and rattlesnake converged to 1.5–2.0 ms at their operating temperatures.
source: Taken together, the FWHM[Ca2+]i values for SFMs in zebra finch, toadfish, and rattlesnake converged to 1.5–2.0 ms at their operating temperatures (Figure 6b).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 6b.

claim: Calcium loading and unloading kinetics in isolated SR vesicles yield similar values for bat SFMs compared to songbird and toadfish SFMs.
source: This technique yields comparable values for SFMs in zebra finch, toadfish and bat, which were significantly elevated (p<0.01, ANOVA) 5–10 times compared to intraspecific skeletal muscle and also compared to the comparable rat fast twitch m. extensor digitorum longus (Figure 6c, Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the results with statistical analysis and supported by data shown in Figure 6c.

claim: Bat larynx SFMs have equally fast calcium dynamics as zebra finch syrinx and toadfish swimbladder SFMs.
source: These data thus suggest that bat larynx SFMs have equally fast calcium dynamics as zebra finch syrinx and toadfish swimbladder SFMs.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on the SR vesicle data.

claim: All established SFMs have similar speeds of calcium dynamics at their operating temperatures in vivo.
source: This in turn implies that all established SFMs have similar speeds of calcium dynamics at their operating temperatures in vivo.
evidence: This is stated in the results as an inference from the calcium dynamics data.

claim: The SFM phenotype found in the sound-producing organs of bats, songbirds, and toadfish descends from different evolutionary events.
source: Since extremely fast crossbridge kinetics are necessary, though not sufficient, for superfast performance (Rome, 2006), and these are set largely by MYH gene expression in vertebrates (Bottinelli et al., 1991), the parsimonious conclusion is that the SFM phenotype found in the sound-producing organs of bats, songbirds, and toadfish descends from different evolutionary events.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a conclusion based on the MYH gene expression data.

claim: All SFMs converge upon identical speed of in vivo calcium dynamics.
source: First, we establish that all SFMs converge upon identical speed of in vivo calcium dynamics, which can be explained by increased SR per myofibril volume ratio.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a summary of the calcium dynamics findings.

claim: Increased SR per myofibril volume ratio explains the identical speed of in vivo calcium dynamics in all SFMs.
source: First, we establish that all SFMs converge upon identical speed of in vivo calcium dynamics, which can be explained by increased SR per myofibril volume ratio.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an explanation for the calcium dynamics convergence.

claim: Actomyosin crossbridge cycling with a higher than normal detachment rate is a hallmark of SFM.
source: Second, actomyosin crossbridge cycling with a higher than normal detachment rate also appears to be a hallmark of SFM, as evidenced by consistently low developed isometric tensions in all cases (Rome, 2006; Elemans et al., 2004, 2008, 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with supporting citations.

claim: The expression of a MYH13 ortholog in zebra finch syrinx SFM is consistent with the human protein's superfast kinetics.
source: The expression of a MYH13 ortholog in zebra finch syrinx SFM is consistent with the human protein's superfast kinetics (Bloemink et al., 2013), but if and how the observed predicted protein sequence differences between zebra finch and human MYH13 orthologs affect crossbridge kinetics remains unknown.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a supporting citation.

claim: SFMs from diverse taxa have remarkably similar maximum performance characteristics (force and cycling frequency).
source: Previous observations show that SFMs from diverse taxa have remarkably similar maximum performance characteristics (force and cycling frequency) (Rome, 2006; Elemans et al., 2004, 2008, 2011; Rome et al., 1996; Moon et al., 2002.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with supporting citations.

claim: The similarity in SFM performance extends to the speed of signal transduction itself within the ECC pathway (calcium release and reuptake).
source: Here, we demonstrate that the similarity extends to the speed of signal transduction itself within the ECC pathway (calcium release and reuptake), and to mechanisms of attaining those speeds (volume and distribution of SR).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a summary of the findings.

claim: The similarity in SFM performance extends to mechanisms of attaining those speeds (volume and distribution of SR).
source: Here, we demonstrate that the similarity extends to the speed of signal transduction itself within the ECC pathway (calcium release and reuptake), and to mechanisms of attaining those speeds (volume and distribution of SR).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a summary of the findings.

claim: The similarities in SFM performance must be attributed to convergent evolution.
source: Because we establish SFM's divergent origin, we propose that these similarities must be attributed to convergent evolution.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a conclusion based on the divergent evolutionary origin.

claim: Female canaries prefer faster trill rates.
source: There is good evidence for selective pressures on high cycling speeds in the motor systems in which SFMs have evolved: female canaries prefer faster trill rates (Drăgănoiu et al., 2002), echolocating bats could produce much higher call rates before introducing call-echo ambiguity to their sensory system (Elemans et al., 2011) and in toadfish call fundamental frequency, which is set 1:1 by muscle speed (Elemans et al., 2014), positively correlates with male fitness (Amorim et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a supporting citation.

claim: In toadfish, call fundamental frequency positively correlates with male fitness.
source: There is good evidence for selective pressures on high cycling speeds in the motor systems in which SFMs have evolved: female canaries prefer faster trill rates (Drăgănoiu et al., 2002), echolocating bats could produce much higher call rates before introducing call-echo ambiguity to their sensory system (Elemans et al., 2011) and in toadfish call fundamental frequency, which is set 1:1 by muscle speed (Elemans et al., 2014), positively correlates with male fitness (Amorim et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with supporting citations.

claim: In toadfish swimbladder SFMs, a trade-off between force-generating capacity and speed is well-established.
source: In toadfish swimbladder SFMs, a trade-off between force-generating capacity and speed is well-established and results from two constraints related to (i) crossbridge dynamics and (ii) increased ECC pathway requirements (Rome, 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a supporting citation.

claim: A lower proportion of myosin motors is bound to actin at a given time in SFMs, reducing the developed force.
source: The consequence of fast relaxation rate is that a lower proportion of myosin motors is bound to actin at a given time reducing the developed force and, by extension, the specific force of the myofibril as a whole (Rome et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a supporting citation.

claim: Detachment rates of intact toadfish SFM fibers are very high.
source: While detachment rates of intact toadfish SFM fibers (Rome et al., 1999) and isolated MYH13 (Bloemink et al., 2013) are very high, attachment rates approximate that of locomotory muscle, and are likely limited by diffusion of the unbound myosin head (Rome et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with supporting citations.

claim: Attachment rates in toadfish SFM approximate that of locomotory muscle and are likely limited by diffusion of the unbound myosin head.
source: While detachment rates of intact toadfish SFM fibers (Rome et al., 1999) and isolated MYH13 (Bloemink et al., 2013) are very high, attachment rates approximate that of locomotory muscle, and are likely limited by diffusion of the unbound myosin head (Rome et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with supporting citations.

claim: The necessity for very rapid ECC signal transduction requires more cell volume dedicated to increased demands on calcium dynamics and ATP production, limiting space for myofibrils.
source: Furthermore, the necessity for very rapid ECC signal transduction requires more cell volume dedicated to increased demands on calcium dynamics and ATP production, limiting space for myofibrils, further diminishing force generation per unit volume of muscle (Rome and Lindstedt, 1998).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a supporting citation.

claim: Additional SR and mitochondria are likely to affect the muscle cell's viscoelastic properties.
source: Importantly, additional SR and mitochondria are likely to affect the muscle cell's viscoelastic properties.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a speculation.

claim: The ultimate limit to how much force can be traded for speed is dictated by the minimum force required to overcome unavoidable viscous losses associated with shortening.
source: The ultimate limit to how much force can be traded for speed, while the muscle still maintains the ability to do external work, is dictated by the minimum force required to overcome unavoidable viscous losses associated with shortening.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a theoretical constraint.

claim: SFMs converge at a maximum speed allowed by fundamental constraints in vertebrate synchronous muscle architecture.
source: Taken together, these observations support the view that SFMs converge at a maximum speed allowed by fundamental constraints in vertebrate synchronous muscle architecture.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a conclusion based on the convergence data.

claim: In insect asynchronous flight muscle, force cycling is uncoupled from calcium cycling, minimizing force loss and allowing for high power production at similar cycling speeds to SFM.
source: In insect asynchronous flight muscle force cycling is uncoupled from calcium cycling, minimizing force loss and allowing for high power production at similar cycling speeds to SFM (Syme and Josephson, 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a supporting citation.

claim: The increase in power at high speeds in insect asynchronous flight muscle is at the great cost of sacrificing precise temporal control of contraction.
source: However, this increase in power at high speeds is at the great cost of sacrificing precise temporal control of contraction (Syme and Josephson, 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a supporting citation.

claim: The cicada's synchronous tymbal muscles cycle at over 500 Hz.
source: The cicada's synchronous tymbal muscles cycle at over 500 Hz (Josephson and Young, 1985), but it is unknown if mass reduction or adaptations to the ECC account for this extreme performance.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a supporting citation.

claim: The low forces developed by SFMs restrict them to low-mass systems as found in sound production and modulation where precise control is essential.
source: In the much larger vertebrates, the low forces developed by SFMs restrict them to low-mass systems as found in sound production and modulation where precise control is essential.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a conclusion.

claim: MYH13 ortholog expression in avian syrinx SFM places syringeal myogenic precursor cells in the craniofacial muscle group.
source: Our discovery of MYH13 ortholog expression in avian syrinx SFM corroborates earlier developmental studies (Noden et al., 1999; Noden and Francis-West, 2006) and places syringeal myogenic precursor cells in the craniofacial muscle group, because this muscle group can uniquely express MYH genes, such as MYH13, 15 and 16, that have never have been found in axial somatic muscle cells.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with supporting citations.

claim: MYH13 expression was progressively upregulated during the sensorimotor period of vocal learning in juvenile songbirds and positively associated with muscle speed.
source: In juvenile songbirds, MYH13 expression was progressively upregulated during the sensorimotor period of vocal learning and positively associated with muscle speed (Figure 4c,d).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by data shown in Figures 4c and 4d.

claim: Neural activity associated with optokinetic and vestibulo-ocular reflexes stimulates particularly MYH13 expression in rat extraocular muscle.
source: In other motor systems, neural stimulation can drive MYH expression patterns: neural activity associated with optokinetic and vestibulo-ocular reflexes stimulates particularly MYH13 expression in rat extraocular muscle (Brueckner et al., 1999; Moncman et al., 2011), and transnervation from cranial nerve X with XII increases speed of laryngeal muscles in dogs (Paniello et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with supporting citations.

claim: In extraocular muscle, MYH13 is found close to the neuromuscular junction.
source: Because in extraocular muscle MYH13 is found close to the neuromuscular junction (Briggs and Schachat, 2002), a possible mechanism could be that both electrical and chemical activation of the motor neuron directly stimulate MYH13 production linked to actetylcholine receptors (Rubinstein et al., 2004; Sanes and Lichtman, 2001).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with supporting citations.

claim: Vocal muscle training can be associated with optimizing SFM function.
source: We speculate that vocal muscle training can be associated with optimizing SFM function.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as speculation.

claim: SFMs can peripherally constrain the precision to execute skilled motor sequences during birdsong and echolocation call ontogeny.
source: Reversely, our data suggest that, next to neural constraints, SFMs can peripherally constrain the precision to execute skilled motor sequences during birdsong and echolocation call ontogeny.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a suggestion based on the data.

claim: Motor-driven acoustic modulation rates in complex communication are fundamentally limited by muscle architecture.
source: Motor-driven acoustic modulation rates in complex communication are thus fundamentally limited by muscle architecture.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a conclusion.

claim: Both MYH13 and MYH4 were the result of gene duplication events that occurred in tetrapods.
source: Our analysis is consistent with earlier findings (Desjardins et al., 2002; Ikeda et al., 2007) that both MYH13 and MYH4 were the result of gene duplication events that occurred in tetrapods, and would, therefore, have no ortholog in the ray-finned fish, the taxon to which the toadfish belongs.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with supporting citations.

claim: MYH13 and MYH4 would have no ortholog in the ray-finned fish.
source: Our analysis is consistent with earlier findings (Desjardins et al., 2002; Ikeda et al., 2007) that both MYH13 and MYH4 were the result of gene duplication events that occurred in tetrapods, and would, therefore, have no ortholog in the ray-finned fish, the taxon to which the toadfish belongs.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an inference from the phylogenetic analysis.

claim: Orthologs of human MYH13 are prime candidates for superfast motor performance.
source: Among known MYH genes, orthologs of human MYH13 are prime candidates for superfast motor performance (Bloemink et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the results with a supporting citation.

claim: In humans and other mammals, MYH13 and five other MYH genes are linked head-to-tail in what is known as the fast/developmental cluster.
source: In humans and other mammals, MYH13 and five other MYH genes (MYH8, MYH4, MYH1, MYH2, MYH3) are linked head-to-tail in what is known as the fast/developmental cluster (Desjardins et al., 2002), which arose from multiple gene duplication events, the first believed to have occurred in an early tetrapod (Ikeda et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the results with supporting citations.

claim: The fast/developmental cluster arose from multiple gene duplication events, the first believed to have occurred in an early tetrapod.
source: In humans and other mammals, MYH13 and five other MYH genes (MYH8, MYH4, MYH1, MYH2, MYH3) are linked head-to-tail in what is known as the fast/developmental cluster (Desjardins et al., 2002), which arose from multiple gene duplication events, the first believed to have occurred in an early tetrapod (Ikeda et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the results with supporting citations.

claim: Phylogenetic analysis revealed orthologs of MYH13 in syntenic genomic regions of all mammalian and avian species included in the analysis.
source: Phylogenetic analysis of myosin rod amino acid sequence revealed orthologs of MYH13 in syntenic genomic regions of all mammalian and avian species included in our analysis corroborating previous studies (Desjardins et al., 2002; Nasipak and Kelley, 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the results with supporting citations.

claim: Some ray-finned fishes, including torafugu, only have a single MYH gene in duplicated genomic regions syntenic to the tetrapod fast/developmental cluster.
source: Some ray-finned fishes, including torafugu, only have a single MYH gene in duplicated genomic regions syntenic to the tetrapod fast/developmental cluster (Ikeda et al., 2007), supporting the view that the duplication event at this locus, which gave rise to an ancestral MYH13 postdated the tetrapod/ray finned fish last common ancestor.
evidence: This is stated in the results with a supporting citation.

claim: The duplication event at the fast/developmental locus, which gave rise to an ancestral MYH13, postdated the tetrapod/ray finned fish last common ancestor.
source: Some ray-finned fishes, including torafugu, only have a single MYH gene in duplicated genomic regions syntenic to the tetrapod fast/developmental cluster (Ikeda et al., 2007), supporting the view that the duplication event at this locus, which gave rise to an ancestral MYH13 postdated the tetrapod/ray finned fish last common ancestor.
evidence: This is stated in the results as an inference from the phylogenetic data.

claim: Laryngeal muscles of the frog, which power vocalizations in the range of 70 Hz, express a MYH gene (MyHC-101d) that does not appear to have descended from the ancestral fast/developmental locus.
source: Interestingly, laryngeal muscles of the frog, which power vocalizations in the range of 70 Hz, express a MYH gene (MyHC-101d) that does not appear to have descended from the ancestral fast/developmental locus (Nasipak and Kelley, 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the results with a supporting citation.

claim: Zebra finch syrinx SFM contained 15 ± 1, 22 ± 2 and 50 ± 2% of SR, mitochondria and myofibrils, respectively.
source: Zebra finch syrinx SFMs contained 15 ± 1, 22 ± 2 and 50 ± 2% of SR, mitochondria and myofibrils, respectively (N = 3) and transmission electron-microscopy images resembled those of dove (Elemans et al., 2006) and oilbird (Suthers and Hector, 1985) syrinx muscles.
evidence: This is stated in the results with measurement values.

claim: Bat larynx SFMs contained 24 ± 2, 31 ± 4 and 34 ± 2% of SR, mitochondria and myofibrils, respectively.
source: Bat larynx SFMs contained 24 ± 2, 31 ± 4 and 34 ± 2% of SR, mitochondria and myofibrils, respectively (N = 2) (Figure 5b).
evidence: This is stated in the results with measurement values and supported by Figure 5b.

claim: The magnitude of [Ca2+]i transients decreased from first to consecutive twitches in toadfish SFM.
source: While the magnitude of the [Ca2+]i transient decreased from first to consecutive twitches confirming earlier work on toadfish SFM (Harwood et al., 2011), the FWHM of the [Ca2+]i transients did not change as a function of twitch number (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results with a supporting citation and shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The FWHM of the [Ca2+]i transients did not change as a function of twitch number in toadfish SFM.
source: While the magnitude of the [Ca2+]i transient decreased from first to consecutive twitches confirming earlier work on toadfish SFM (Harwood et al., 2011), the FWHM of the [Ca2+]i transients did not change as a function of twitch number (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: In zebra finch SFMs, there was no significant magnitude or FWHM decrease of [Ca2+]i transients as a function of twitch number.
source: In zebra finch SFMs, there was no significant magnitude (KW, p>0.05) or FWHM decrease (KW, p>0.05) of [Ca2+]i transients as a function of twitch number (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results with statistical analysis and shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Female zebra finch syringeal SFMs have two-fold slower twitch kinetics than male syringeal SFMs.
source: Female syringeal SFMs have two-fold slower twitch kinetics than male syringeal SFMs (Elemans et al., 2008), and expressed more than five times less MYH13 compared to male syringeal SFMs (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is stated in the results with a supporting citation.

claim: Levels of MYH13 expression in zebra finch syrinx SFM are negatively associated with twitch duration and thus positively with muscle speed.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that in zebra finch syrinx SFM levels of MYH13 expression are negatively associated with twitch duration and thus positively with muscle speed.
evidence: This is stated in the results as a conclusion from the developmental data.

claim: The SFM in the larynx of juvenile bats may increase speed during the first 30 days after birth as suggested by an increase in frequency modulation speed of echolocation calls.
source: Interestingly, the SFM in the larynx of juvenile bats may also increase speed during the first 30 days after birth as suggested by an increase in frequency modulation speed of echolocation calls (Moss et al., 1997).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a supporting citation.

claim: Transnervation from cranial nerve X with XII increases speed of laryngeal muscles in dogs.
source: In other motor systems, neural stimulation can drive MYH expression patterns: neural activity associated with optokinetic and vestibulo-ocular reflexes stimulates particularly MYH13 expression in rat extraocular muscle (Brueckner et al., 1999; Moncman et al., 2011), and transnervation from cranial nerve X with XII increases speed of laryngeal muscles in dogs (Paniello et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a supporting citation.

claim: Both electrical and chemical activation of the motor neuron may directly stimulate MYH13 production linked to acetylcholine receptors.
source: Because in extraocular muscle MYH13 is found close to the neuromuscular junction (Briggs and Schachat, 2002), a possible mechanism could be that both electrical and chemical activation of the motor neuron directly stimulate MYH13 production linked to actetylcholine receptors (Rubinstein et al., 2004; Sanes and Lichtman, 2001).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a possible mechanism with supporting citations.

claim: The zebra finch MYH13 ortholog differs from those of both human and chicken by the substitution of a proline at position 210 in loop 1.
source: Although human MYH13 is known to possess rapid ADP dissociation (Bloemink et al., 2013), the zebra finch ortholog differs from those of both human and chicken by the substitution of a proline at position 210.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on sequence alignment analysis.

claim: Both zebra finch MYH13 and bat MYH4 possess amino acid substitutions in loop two.
source: Both zebra finch MYH13 and bat MYH4 possess amino acid substitutions in loop two and in the case of the finch the insertion of a glycine at position 643 not shared by chicken, flying fox, or human orthologs.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on sequence alignment analysis.

claim: Zebra finch MYH13 has an insertion of a glycine at position 643 in loop two not shared by chicken, flying fox, or human orthologs.
source: Both zebra finch MYH13 and bat MYH4 possess amino acid substitutions in loop two and in the case of the finch the insertion of a glycine at position 643 not shared by chicken, flying fox, or human orthologs.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on sequence alignment analysis.

claim: The only non-synonymous sequence difference between little brown bat and human MYH4 in loop 1 is an insertion of a glycine at position 214, which is also shared with the large flying fox.
source: The only non-synonymous sequence difference between little brown bat and human MYH4 in loop 1, an insertion of a glycine at position 214, is also shared with the large flying fox.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on sequence alignment analysis.

claim: Extraocular muscle expressed MYH13 at the same level as syringeal SFM in zebra finch.
source: Extraocular muscle expressed MYH13 at the same level as syringeal SFM (p=0.06, Kruskal Wallis), and also four additional MYH genes from the fast/developmental cluster (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is stated in the results with statistical analysis and shown in Figure 4a.

claim: Zebra finch extraocular muscle expressed four additional MYH genes from the fast/developmental cluster in addition to MYH13.
source: Extraocular muscle expressed MYH13 at the same level as syringeal SFM (p=0.06, Kruskal Wallis), and also four additional MYH genes from the fast/developmental cluster (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 4a.

claim: Loop one is situated near the nucleotide binding pocket, and its flexibility is thought to influence the rate of ADP dissociation.
source: Loop one is situated near the nucleotide binding pocket, and its flexibility is thought to influence the rate of ADP dissociation, and thus is a potentially critical region for the rapid crossbridge detachment seen in SFM (Ikeda et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the results with a supporting citation.

claim: Loop two potentially affects maximum shortening velocity via influence on actin-myosin binding.
source: Loop two potentially affects maximum shortening velocity via influence on actin-myosin binding (Lorenz and Holmes, 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the results with a supporting citation.

claim: Human MYH13 is known to possess rapid ADP dissociation.
source: Although human MYH13 is known to possess rapid ADP dissociation (Bloemink et al., 2013), the zebra finch ortholog differs from those of both human and chicken by the substitution of a proline at position 210.
evidence: This is stated in the results with a supporting citation.

claim: Detachment rates of isolated MYH13 are very high.
source: While detachment rates of intact toadfish SFM fibers (Rome et al., 1999) and isolated MYH13 (Bloemink et al., 2013) are very high, attachment rates approximate that of locomotory muscle, and are likely limited by diffusion of the unbound myosin head (Rome et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a supporting citation.

claim: Echolocating bats could produce much higher call rates before introducing call-echo ambiguity to their sensory system.
source: There is good evidence for selective pressures on high cycling speeds in the motor systems in which SFMs have evolved: female canaries prefer faster trill rates (Drăgănoiu et al., 2002), echolocating bats could produce much higher call rates before introducing call-echo ambiguity to their sensory system (Elemans et al., 2011) and in toadfish call fundamental frequency, which is set 1:1 by muscle speed (Elemans et al., 2014), positively correlates with male fitness (Amorim et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a supporting citation.

claim: In toadfish, call fundamental frequency is set 1:1 by muscle speed.
source: There is good evidence for selective pressures on high cycling speeds in the motor systems in which SFMs have evolved: female canaries prefer faster trill rates (Drăgănoiu et al., 2002), echolocating bats could produce much higher call rates before introducing call-echo ambiguity to their sensory system (Elemans et al., 2011) and in toadfish call fundamental frequency, which is set 1:1 by muscle speed (Elemans et al., 2014), positively correlates with male fitness (Amorim et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a supporting citation.

claim: Calcium loading and unloading kinetics in isolated SR vesicles were significantly elevated 5–10 times in SFMs compared to intraspecific skeletal muscle.
source: This technique yields comparable values for SFMs in zebra finch, toadfish and bat, which were significantly elevated (p<0.01, ANOVA) 5–10 times compared to intraspecific skeletal muscle and also compared to the comparable rat fast twitch m. extensor digitorum longus (Figure 6c, Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the results with statistical analysis and shown in Figure 6c.

claim: Calcium loading and unloading kinetics in isolated SR vesicles of SFMs were significantly elevated compared to rat fast twitch m. extensor digitorum longus.
source: This technique yields comparable values for SFMs in zebra finch, toadfish and bat, which were significantly elevated (p<0.01, ANOVA) 5–10 times compared to intraspecific skeletal muscle and also compared to the comparable rat fast twitch m. extensor digitorum longus (Figure 6c, Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the results with statistical analysis and shown in Figure 6c.
